endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Establish protocols for escalating and communicating concerns/incidents for resolution to the governance structure.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: This includes verifying that responsible parties are able to access relevant social, ethical, legal, human factors and/or clinical stakeholders/advisers in the event that specific problems arise.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Practice and follow incident response plans for addressing the generation of inappropriate or harmful content and adapt processes based on findings to prevent future occurrences.

endorsements.title: Generative AI for pre-consultation mental health triage in disorders of gut-brain interaction
endorsements.quote: At minimum, a pre-agreed escalation protocol should specify: (a) the named clinical role responsible for review (e.g., duty gastroenterologist, clinical nurse specialist, or on-call liaison psychiatry); (b) a maximum review window (e.g., within 4 hours during working hours, or a defined out-of-hours pathway); (c) the clinical channel through which escalation occurs (e.g., direct notification to the electronic health record task list with audit trail, or direct phone contact for imminent risk); and (d) a documented fallback procedure when the primary reviewer is unavailable, including escalation to the next designated role.

endorsements.title: Generative AI as interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life
endorsements.quote: Local workflows defining thresholds, reviewer roles, response time, documentation, and feedback loops after a flag is generated.

endorsements.title: A Responsible AI Readiness Framework for Digital Self-Management Platforms: Illustrative Application to a Rule-Based GERD Platform
endorsements.quote: Safety requires explicit red flags, contraindications, medication boundaries, escalation and adverse-event procedures, limits of automated advice, and named responsibility for reviewing, overriding, suspending, or investigating system behavior.

commentary.bottom_line: Six sources, including CHAI playbooks and the NIST generative AI profile, endorse named owners, escalation channels, and timed severity tiers for AI concerns, but no supplied study tests this practice or documents the stalled-escalation hazard it targets. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: The supplied evidence contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. All six endorsements come from frameworks or commentaries. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the strength of the endorsements should not be read as a measure of effectiveness.

CHAI's governance playbook labels escalation protocols a must, and NIST AI 600-1 advises practicing incident response plans for harmful generated content. These are voluntary frameworks, and the supplied material cites no statute or rule that requires specific tiers or timeframes.

Two commentaries propose concrete elements, such as a named clinical reviewer and a maximum review window of about 4 hours during working hours. No supplied study measures whether such windows shorten time to resolution or prevent harm, so the proposed timeframes remain untested design choices.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or units with and without named triage owners and severity-tiered timeframes on outcomes such as time from AI concern to governance review, time to resolution, recurrence of incidents, or patient harm. No study establishes how often AI concerns stall in the absence of these structures.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether escalation channels capture concerns raised by or about these patients, including concerns reported in languages other than English, is unknown.
